nameStory: The swollen bladderwort gets its name from the distinctive inflated or 'swollen' appearance of its floating stems, which look like tiny balloons helping the plant stay afloat. The 'bladderwort' part comes from the hundreds of tiny bladder-like traps hidden underwater that work like miniature vacuum cleaners to catch prey. These inflated floats make it the most buoyant member of its carnivorous family!
description: Swollen bladderwort is a fascinating floating carnivorous plant that drifts on the surface of quiet ponds and lakes. The most noticeable feature is its ring of inflated, spongy stems that act like a life preserver, keeping bright yellow snapdragon-like flowers held high above the water. Beneath the surface, feathery underwater leaves hide hundreds of microscopic traps that catch tiny water creatures. This impressive aquatic hunter can form large floating mats several feet across.

idTips.label: Inflated Stems
idTips.description: The distinctive ring of swollen, spongy stems feels like squeezing a foam pool noodle and keeps the plant floating like a natural life ring - this is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers shaped like tiny snapdragons rise 4-6 inches above the water on a single stalk, with a distinctive lower lip that serves as a landing pad for pollinators

idTips.label: Underwater Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery, highly divided leaves beneath the surface feel soft and delicate to the touch, resembling green underwater ferns with thread-like segments

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms large floating mats that can cover significant portions of pond surfaces, with individual plants connecting to create carpet-like colonies

idTips.label: Bladder Traps
idTips.description: Tiny clear bladders less than 1/8 inch long are scattered along the underwater leaves, visible with close inspection as small translucent pouches

habitat: Found in quiet, acidic ponds, shallow lakes, and slow-moving backwaters throughout New England, though it's more common in southeastern Massachusetts. Prefers nutrient-poor waters with soft bottoms where it can anchor initially before becoming free-floating. Often found alongside other aquatic plants like water lilies and pickerelweed in areas with minimal water movement.

seasonality.spring: Plants begin growing from winter buds and developing their characteristic inflated stems as water temperatures warm. New growth emerges from overwintering turions (specialized winter buds) at the pond bottom.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers most visible from June through August. This is the best time to spot the distinctive inflated stems and floating mats at their largest size.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants begin forming winter buds called turions. The floating portions may start to break apart and sink as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Plants overwinter as turions (winter buds) resting on the pond bottom, completely invisible until spring warmth triggers new growth. No above-water portions remain during freezing months.

funFact: Each plant can have over 1,000 tiny bladder traps that work like underwater vacuum cleaners, sucking in prey in less than a millisecond - making them among the fastest traps in the plant kingdom and turning this delicate floating flower into one of nature's most efficient microscopic predators!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small swollen bladderwort, but swollen bladderwort is significantly larger with more prominent inflated stems that feel notably spongy when squeezed. Memory trick: 'swollen' means bigger - if the inflated stems are really obvious and the whole plant is impressive in size, it's the swollen bladderwort, not its smaller cousin.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being native to southeastern United States, swollen bladderwort has been spreading northward since the 1980s and is now considered potentially invasive in some New England waters. Its ability to form dense mats can alter local pond ecosystems, making it one of the few carnivorous plants that can actually become a problematic species.
compareHints: Swollen bladderwort is the largest of New England's aquatic bladderworts and the only one with truly prominent inflated stems that feel spongy to the touch. Common bladderwort lacks the inflated stems entirely, while small swollen bladderwort has much smaller, less noticeable inflated portions. The ring-like arrangement of puffy stems makes swollen bladderwort unmistakable among its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Horned bladderwort stands out from its many bladderwort relatives by having the most prominent horn-like spur and by growing in terrestrial or semi-aquatic conditions rather than fully underwater.
Small swollen bladderwort is smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort and lacks the large inflated floats of swollen bladderwort.
Among New England's bladderworts, purple bladderwort is unique for its purple flowers – most others have yellow blooms.
Common bladderwort is the largest and most robust of New England's bladderworts, with the biggest flowers and most substantial underwater growth.
Intermediate bladderwort differs from common bladderwort by having fewer, slightly smaller flowers and more delicate overall appearance.
Humped bladderwort is much smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort, forming thin surface mats rather than robust underwater colonies.
Northeastern bladderwort is distinguished from other New England bladderworts by its lavender-purple flowers and preference for very shallow water or bog margins.

Hidden-fruit Bladderwort is unique among New England's bladderworts for keeping its flowers at or below the water surface, while most relatives like Common and Purple Bladderwort hold their blooms well above water on conspicuous stalks.
Lesser bladderwort is distinguished from common bladderwort by its much smaller size and more delicate appearance overall.
Among New England's bladderworts, zigzag bladderwort is unique for its terrestrial zigzag growth habit - most other bladderworts either float in water or grow upright from water.
Distinguished from common bladderwort by much finer, more delicate underwater stems and smaller overall size.
